## 7. Hostile validation (HV) and review

Review and hostile-validation (HV) guidance (operator-directed, 2026-10-09). Applies to every agent, plan, and review loop.

### 7.1 Adversarial review of tracked results (locked 2026-08-12)

1. Validate independently through a hostile reviewer wherever the plan calls for HV and before any done state (section 4.5). Self-check alone is not validation.
2. Every result is timestamped with a sortable local date and time (section 3.1).
3. Every FAIL and UNKNOWN from the review is shown to the operator.
4. Every result includes an accuracy rating and a completeness rating.

Reviewer (resolution of 2026-10-13, verbatim): "HV must not be executed by the same agent family as the requesting agent.  If not specified by operator, ask what agent and model to use for HV in a session." HV uses the reviewer and tooling explicitly authorized for the session. Verify the reviewer's model and effort from its own runtime receipts.

Review time is unbounded (operator, 2026-10-12, verbatim: "Do not bound review time"): no timeout, kill, deadline, or wait limit on any HV reviewer run, and no expected duration in briefs or plans; the implementer only checks the response stream in repeated read-only waits until the run completes, however long the review takes.

When HV runs (resolution of 2026-10-13, verbatim): "HV cadence is an artifact of the plan, not a standing rule." Section 4.5 still requires hostile AGREE before any done state.

### 7.2 Mandatory scope (locked 2026-08-13; operations versus requirements locked 2026-08-14)

Operator directive (verbatim intent): hostile validation must test for workspace rule violations, requirement violations, and the current plan holistically, in addition to the requested validation. Mandatory attack surfaces on every run:
1. Requested validation: every implementer claim (pass, done, green, fixed, SHAs, test counts, receipts).
2. Workspace rules: honesty, receipts, MCP-only TODO, session, and requirement storage when the workspace uses the MCP server, PowerShell only, no Python. BDPv4 and related directives pertain only to code and documentation in the scope of implementing the project. Phase order (requirements drive tests; tests before implementation) is caught by a hostile review between phases of plan implementation. Do not fail it solely by comparing FR `createdAt` to test or implementation file times after the slice is written. Do not apply BDPv4 to user-directed operations.
3. Requirements: apply to project requirement work only (product features, implementation, claimed-complete plan steps). FR, TR, TEST, AC, and mappings are required there; missing FR, TR, or AC for claimed-complete implementation work is FAIL.
4. Current plan holistically: when the implementer claims plan-step completion, check the plan's definition of done, blockers, amendments, and exit criteria. A user-directed operational action does not have to satisfy an unrelated plan's definition of done unless it claimed that plan step done.

Two work classes:
1. Project implementation scope: product code, product tests, project documentation, and plan-step completion for that implementation. BDPv4 and related directives pertain only to this class. Missing FR, TR, TEST, or AC for claimed-complete implementation work is FAIL on surface 3.
2. User-directed general actions: operator-ordered lab or operations work that is not a product requirement (for example: uninstall an obsolete package, back up a device, pair wireless ADB, take a screenshot, copy a store the operator named, remove a leftover launcher). These are not FR, TR, or TEST. Surface 3 must not FAIL for "no FR or TR for this uninstall" or equivalent.

How the reviewer classifies: classify the request first and record the class on the receipt. If the operator explicitly directed the action, default to class 2 unless the implementer also shipped product code or claimed a plan or FR complete. Do not invent a requirements gap to punish class-2 work. If class-2 work is mixed with class-1 product changes in the same turn, score them separately and FAIL surface 3 only on the class-1 slice. What still applies to class-2 work: surface 1 (did they do the directed action, with receipts), surface 2 (honesty, receipts, look before delete, PowerShell, no Python, MCP-only storage; not BDPv4 for the operation itself), and surface 4 only if they claim an active plan step is complete.

OverallVerdict is AGREE only if all applicable surfaces PASS; surface 3 is not applicable (not a FAIL) for class-2 operator actions. A parent agent must not under-scope the brief to code-only claims on class-1 work; if it does, the reviewer expands and still evaluates the applicable surfaces. A code-only brief that omits BDPv4, requirements, or the plan is non-compliant.

The reviewer executes the add-profile skill before beginning its validation work, every run including resume, and its receipt records that it ran.

### 7.3 Score gate and the bar (locked 2026-09-10)

A hostile validation passes only when both its accuracy score and completeness score are at least 98 percent. Any individual score below 98 is a failure; OverallVerdict must be DISAGREE when either score is below 98, even if the FAIL and UNKNOWN counts are both zero. If a reviewer emits a verdict without numeric accuracy and completeness scores, the HV is incomplete: treat it as DISAGREE until scores are present and at least 98. The threshold is an acceptance threshold, not a target reviewers may game or inflate. A sub-98 score cannot authorize any goal, TODO, requirement, or plan done-state change: display it as a failure, remediate, and rerun.

98/98 HV (accuracy and completeness) is the bar for a functioning system, not perfection. Never lower, skip, or approve below it; lower thresholds let real bugs through that later become blocking test failures. When rounds stop converging, fix the process, never the threshold. "98/98 is not perfection, it is functional." Never propose lowering it (added 2026-10-13, from the operator's ruling of 2026-10-09).

### 7.4 Receipts and the session log (locked 2026-09-10)

Operator directive (verbatim intent): HV requests must have request and response logged as jsonl files; the results of HV validation must be saved in their entirety to the MCP session log.

1. Request jsonl: one JSON object per line covering the HV ask as sent: sortable local timestamp, workspace path, reviewer identity (agent, model, effort), launch command, prompt or body, named evidence paths, and the gate or TODO under review.
2. Response jsonl: the reviewer's full machine stream as jsonl (for a CLI reviewer, its full event stream, every start, tool, message, and completion line; for a subagent reviewer, one object per reviewer message or tool result, then a final object with the complete verdict).
3. Durable locations, in order: the workspace `docs/receipts/hv/{timestamp}-{gate}.request.jsonl` and `.response.jsonl` ({timestamp} is the sortable local date and time in file-safe form, yyyyMMddTHHmmss); otherwise a durable user-level receipts directory named for the workspace. Never only a temp or scratch tree that can be wiped.
4. Build jsonl from native objects and serialize. PowerShell only; no Python; no handwritten JSON.
5. The reviewer's session-log turn stores the entire result: the complete verdict prose, every finding, every PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN item, the scores, OverallVerdict, thread, session, and request ids, the complete VERDICT JSON object, absolute paths to the request and response jsonl, and proof the turn persisted (a history query or equivalent). If a field is too large for one write, split it across ordered dialog or action items on the same turn; never omit findings to fit. The jsonl files remain the byte-complete stream; the session log still carries the full verdict text, not a digest.
6. Every reviewer creates complete session-log turns for every review: bootstrap if needed, open a dedicated review session or a clear review turn, begin the turn, append dialog and actions with integer order values, complete or fail the turn, and prove persistence in the receipt. A review without a complete session-log turn is incomplete, even if its claim verdicts would pass.
7. Progress entries (MEMORY-PREFERENCE-003, verbatim; added 2026-10-13 from PAYTON-LEGION2): "For every future hostile validation (HV) session, require the reviewer to emit progress entries into its durable response JSONL during the run at meaningful intervals, not backfill or consolidate them at the end. Each progress entry must include a numeric completion percentage and an estimated time remaining (ETA). Include this requirement in every HV launch prompt and preserve the entries in the durable response JSONL." The reviewer's ETA is its own report; it never becomes a timeout or a bound on review time (section 7.1).

Forbidden: HV with no request jsonl or no response jsonl; HV whose only record is temp or scratch; AGREE without accuracy and completeness both at or above 98; summarizing HV into the session log instead of storing the entire result; marking a goal, TODO, or plan done on incomplete HV.

### 7.5 Before every HV round

- Read the whole plan and every document under review end to end; targeted checks are not holistic. When the operator asks for a reconciliation or projection of problems before HV, present every projected problem to the operator and get confirmation before launching the review (added 2026-10-13, from the operator's rulings of 2026-10-12 and 2026-10-13).
- Run a structured what-if pass per requirement, not only a consistency check. Ask what observably happens under: crash, restart, or replay at each step; ordering and concurrency; boundary and malformed input; each host or plugin, including unsupported ones; lifecycle (clear, resume, end, terminal states); isolation (cross-workspace, cross-session, cross-agent); legacy and upgrade; operator-visible output. Where the plan does not state the outcome, add a valid AC tagged with the plan's phase or slice and a named test. Adding a valid AC is always a win.
- Chain rules together to find deadlocks: rules that each pass alone but together leave no accepted remedy.
- Diff against known-good anchors and ask "How did it deviate? How do we get back in line?": (1) the operator's verbatim decisions, (2) current working code and baseline-green behavior, (3) classic patterns such as idempotency keys, transactional outbox with at-least-once delivery and idempotent consumers (never claim exactly-once), write-ahead journal before mutation, optimistic concurrency. Justify any departure explicitly or return to the pattern.
- Check that every field set and code list is defined once and identically everywhere, every mapping edge is backed by a TEST statement and vice ver

sa, and handoff and TODO metadata match the plan.
- Edit only between rounds, never while a round is running.
- Propagation audit: after changing any rule, field set, code, or outcome, search every place that states it (requirements, ACs, TRs, TESTs, wire contracts, use cases, the plan's phase or slice tasks, host tables, handoff, TODO) and update each one, or replace the copies with a reference to one canonical statement. In one review round, three of six findings were rules changed in one place and left stale elsewhere. Large edit batches need this audit most.
- Prefer a traceable key over content matching when pairing records (for example queue position or a shared id rather than a text hash); content can differ in representation between producers.
- Search before adding, and lint mechanically: before writing any new rule, grep the whole document for an existing rule on the same subject; a second rule is a contradiction even if each is fine alone (one round added a two-AC TEST rule beside an existing three-AC one). Check cross-reference classes (FR->TR->TEST mappings, which of the plan's phases or slices owns each named case, phase order) with a small script instead of waiting for the reviewer to find them one per round.
- Enforce the checklist, do not just remember it (operator, 2026-10-10, after this guidance was skipped for many unsupervised rounds): make the pre-HV checklist a hard gate in the HV launcher, which refuses a round unless a per-round self-review record shows evidence for each item (holistic review, what-if, propagation audit, phase boundaries, search-before-adding, no new mechanism, mapping lint, the operator scoping directive verbatim in the brief, standing rules in every delegated brief). Guidance that only lives in memory gets skipped under time pressure.
- Phase-boundary audit: every test or AC you add must be allocated to the plan's phase or slice where everything it depends on already exists (server gate, review verbs, marker fields). A behaviour that ships before its dependency needs an explicit activation contract (for example a server-written capability) and an inert mode, including after a rollback. Check the dependency chain and the rollout order for each new case, not just the AC text.

### 7.6 When findings come back

- Ask "What did I miss?", not only "How do I fix this?". Classify each finding (crash window, cross-session addressing, traceability drift, field-set drift, use case vs requirement contradiction, metadata drift, and so on) and sweep the whole artifact for siblings of each class before the next round.
- Verify each finding against source before acting.
- Separate implementer fixes from operator decisions, and batch operator decisions into one question.
- Recurrence signal: when one design area produces new findings in round after round, the problem is structural, usually a missing traceable key or a missing single source of truth. Stop patching. Diff the area against the known-good pattern (for example single writer, one ordered log, idempotency key), return to it, and delete the mechanism the patches added. One design area failed for five rounds until a single minter reading one ordered log replaced the patches.
- Indistinguishable inputs: when two histories produce byte-identical inputs (a redelivery of one event versus a separate event with equal fields), no derived key can separate them. Adding per-invocation state such as a counter or salt breaks idempotence instead. Run the what-if on both histories, then state the honest limit: fail closed under an existing rule, probe how often it happens, and document it. Never promise two invariants the inputs cannot support. Before a fix, check it against every invariant the old value satisfied (purity, retry reuse, the two-process tests), not only the finding it repairs.

### 7.7 Writing fixes

- Fix the deficient requirement. Reconcile with existing requirements first, strengthen an existing AC second, create a new requirement only when the need is genuinely new.
- Do not add design mechanism (protocols, algorithms, crash choreography) to plan text. State the observable, testable outcome; the how belongs to the contract step of the plan's phase or slice.
- Make each fix minimal, then attack it yourself before the next round; fixes are the main source of new findings. Do not churn text that a prior round accepted.

### 7.8 Design principle and coordination

- Always have a traceable relationship when coordinating two disparate entities: every record, event, or message carries the root ids of whatever it is a child of or depends on, so it is attributable on its own. A missing parent id is a design failure. Find the commonality first when relating something new to existing knowledge. Where an external format lacks the key, say so and compensate in your own records; never infer it silently.
- Coordinating with another agent: use one append-only channel with read-back verification (the global memory MEMORY-PROCESS-007 is that channel). Accept counters that expose real defects; fold refinements in only as minimal ACs. Each effort keeps its own required reviewer and gates; keep cross-effort dependencies acyclic and order-independent. A decision relayed by one agent may not satisfy the other agent's approval controls; the operator may need to state it to each agent directly.

Read them in full at session start and carry them verbatim; do not keep a copy of them in this profile (resolution of 2026-10-13: "Reference, don't copy"). The one exception is section 6.4.

- Never print or commit secrets; redact HV streams before committing, because reviewers read marker files.

### 8.1 Who logs what

- Agents always log (added 2026-10-13; operator, verbatim: "BG agents should NEVER skip logging.  NEVER."): every agent that does work (a subagent, a background agent, a reviewer) opens, updates, and completes its own session-log turn through the plugin route and reports its session and request ids; no brief may tell an agent to stay out of the session log.
- One turn per real request, per agent (resolution of 2026-10-13: "Per request, per agent"): each agent logs one turn for each real request it handles; a subagent's turn carries the parent turn's session and request ids (section 7.8), so the work is attributable without counting the request twice. Replace real turns canceled by a later open.
- A background event with no work of its own (a completion notice) is not an agent: its hook-opened turn is failed as system_event_phantom, and the work it reports is logged by the agent that does it (resolution of 2026-10-13: "Events aren't agents").

### 8.2 Decisions are conclusions

In the session log, decisions are conclusions and judgments with their consequences, not the steps taken. They go in the turn's design decisions, distinct from its actions. Every sync or wrap-up pass enumerates the real judgment calls of the turn and logs them. Never report "0 decisions (folded into actions)"; that phrasing is the failure mode itself.

Why: the operator has been trying to get agents to log session decisions reliably since February 2026. The pattern: the keystroke trail (actions) gets captured while the reasoning (design decisions) is under-recorded or buried inside action text. He pays for the reasoning, not just the steps. On 2026-06-29 the first sync pass of a 12-round review loop logged 0 decisions and called them "folded into actions", exactly the gap he has been fighting. He flagged it directly: "Decisions are about your conclusions, not the actions you take" and "It feels like you have been deliberately avoiding session logging... especially details of decisions."

How to apply: on every sync or wrap-up, after appending actions, explicitly list the conclusions made this turn, each as judgment plus consequence plus affected requirements or files, and write them to design decisions, append-only (read existing first, send existing plus new, preserve order). A turn that made genuine judgment calls but logs zero decisions is a red flag; re-check before reporting. Heavy reads can time out and render existing decisions blank; that is a read artifact, not an empty section, so re-read before assuming you must recreate. Write the decision when it happens; do not reconstruct it later.

### 8.3 Turn titles summarize the request

Session-log turn titles are a concise summary of the operator's request: never the literal placeholder "User prompt", and not a verbatim first-line truncation of the prompt.

Why: the operator reviews the session log by turn title; "User prompt" and raw first lines make turns unscannable and indistinguishable.

How to apply: when opening, updating, or completing a turn, set the title to a short request summary. The plugin's prompt hook auto-titles from the prompt's first line and falls back to "User prompt" on empty prompts (Stop-hook continuation turns hit this); the hook cannot summarize, so the agent must refine the title. Never leave a turn titled "User prompt".

16: ## 1. Scope, relationship to the foundation, and precedence
17: 
18: - Scope: the durable, multi-agent hostile validation (HV) pipeline the foundation deferred (foundation section 3.1, "Model grade": "We are going to add an HV pipeline in the future, but not in this effort."). The pipeline admits HV requests over session-log turns, schedules them across a pool of five reviewer agents, runs each review as a durable, leased, live-streamed execution, keeps complete compressed evidence, and finalizes per-turn and holistic results in one transaction.
19: - Relationship: the foundation stays the authority for turn logging (Phase A), turn reviews (Phase B), and stateless agent context (Phase C). This amendment adds one bounded context, HostileValidation, and amends the foundation clauses listed in section 6, which are exactly the clauses that assume a manual HV with one configured grader.
20: - Precedence: where section 6 names a foundation clause as amended, the amendment's text governs; every other foundation clause stands unchanged. Because the foundation's plan (PLAN-SESSIONTURNREVIEW-001) was approved on 2026-10-10, the amended clauses are a change to that plan, and the foundation's own rule applies to them: "a change to this document after the plan is approved is a plan change that needs a new hostile validation" (foundation, introduction).
21: - Implementation status of the foundation (verified 2026-10-16 by a search of `src` at `36783b79`): of the foundation's new types only `IDispatcher` exists (`src/QBrainAi.Cqrs/IDispatcher.cs:9`); `SerializableWrite`, `IdempotentCreate`, `ReadableKeyAllocator`, `TurnLocator`, `ScoreLexeme`, `ScoreVerdict`, `ClassifiedErrorException`, `WorkspaceResolutionBehavior`, `RecordSessionTurnReviewCommand`, `CreateAgentContextHvRequestCommand`, and `RecordModelGradeCommand` are architecture only. Every amendment of section 6 is therefore a document change; no migration of an existing table or route is involved.

24: ## 2. Goals and non-goals
25: 
26: Goals:
27: 
28: 1. A durable HV queue whose admission, scheduling, ownership, and finalization survive server restarts, worker crashes, and concurrent workers without losing or duplicating a review result.
29: 2. A reviewer pool of five agents (Cline, Copilot, Claude, Codex, Grok), selected round-robin among the ready reviewers, never the submitter, the agent that wrote the reviewed turns, or an alias of either.
30: 3. Complete evidence: the complete accepted request and the complete response log of every review, compressed at rest with GZIP, verified lossless, retained until explicitly removed, and streamed live while the review runs.
31: 4. Per-turn assessments and a separate holistic evaluation for every request, committed atomically with the turns' hostile reviews; reviewed turns and final results are immutable.
32: 5. Independence: an agent's self-review never affects HV admission, execution, or verdict, and an HV verdict never completes a TODO.
33: 
34: Non-goals (each settled by the operator, section 3): access roles; a force re-review flag; automatic TODO state changes; automatic retention expiry; execution time limits; a second HV verdict store beside this one for turn reviews.

133: Trust boundaries:
134: 
135: - Callers authenticate with the workspace API key, as every route does; there are no access roles (S-29). Agent identity is therefore not authenticated by the server: the submitter's identity is the agent of the submitting turn the server finds (R-08), and the limit of that model is stated in section 8.
136: - The reviewer CLI is untrusted input to the server. Its output is evidence to verify, never an instruction; the server parses only the records the reviewer contract defines (section 13.3) and verifies them before anything is finalized (policy HvFinalVerification, section 15).
137: - Turn text sent to a reviewer passes through `SecretRedactor` (foundation section 3.5.2) before it leaves the server; the stored request evidence is the redacted brief exactly as sent.

139: ## 5. Design decisions and resolutions
140: 
141: Each resolution names the settled requirements it implements, its rationale, and the alternatives it rejects. Resolutions are proposals for the operator's approval; the settled requirements of section 3 are not reopened.
142: 
143: - R-01 One bounded context. HostileValidation owns the pipeline and is not gated by `Mcp:AgentContext:Mode`: HV of turns works in every Mode, because the operator's HV requirements (S-01 to S-30) name turns, not agent-context responses. Rejected: extending the foundation's `AgentContextHvRequest` in ResponsesAndTrust (draft 103), because that record is mode-gated (foundation section 3.5.1) and lists responses, not turns, so a turn with no response would silently drop out of review (draft 213, "turn coverage versus response coverage").
144: - R-02 The HV request replaces the foundation's agent-context HV request. `HvRequest` keeps the foundation's key format `hvr-<sessionId>-<yyyyMMddTHHmmssZ>` (with `-<nn>` from the second key of one second, ReadableKeyAllocator) and lists turns (`HvRequestTurn`); the agent responses of those turns are linked as `HvRequestResponse` items when Phase C has recorded any. CreateAgentContextHvRequestCommand, GetAgentContextHvRequestQuery, QueryAgentContextHvRequestsQuery, and their entities are superseded (amendment A-04). Rejected: keeping two HV request records (one per turn, one per response), which would need a cross-record consistency rule the foundation never needed.
145: - R-03 Model grades come from finalization only. FinalizeHvRequestCommand dispatches the foundation's RecordModelGradeCommand for each linked response inside its own transaction; the public model-grade route, the two-step `codex exec resume` protocol, and `ModelGrader:*` are removed, and the eight receipt checks become the verification steps V-1 to V-8 of policy HvFinalVerification against evidence the server itself captured (amendment A-05). Rationale: the pipeline launches the reviewer and records its complete output, so the server no longer has to trust receipts written by a runner it did not control. Rejected: keeping the reviewer-submitted grade route beside the pipeline, which would let a grade bypass reviewer exclusion and atomic finalization (S-17, S-23).
146: - R-04 Freeze at admission, finality at finalization (S-06, S-07). Admission sets each member turn's HV state to `Pending` in the same transaction that creates the request; finalization sets it to `Final`. Every write to a `Pending` or `Final` turn or its children, from every surface and origin, is refused with 409 `turn_immutable` and `details.reason` `hv_pending` or `hv_final` (policy HvTurnFreeze), except the one write of finalization itself (origin `HvFinalization`). A request that ends `Canceled` or `Failed` releases its turns back to `None`. Rationale: the reviewed content equals the finalized content without a content comparison race, and the operator's "may not allow updates" is one guard in the existing write path. Rejected: letting writes continue and refusing finalization on a changed snapshot hash, which would waste completed reviews and still leave a window between the last check and the commit.
147: - R-05 Only terminal turns are admitted. A member turn that is not terminal (`TurnStatus.IsTerminal`, foundation section 3.5.3) refuses the whole request with 409 `hv_turns_not_terminal`, naming each turn. The submitting turn is never a member: a session scope excludes it and reports the exclusion in the result, and a turn or range scope that names it is refused with 400 `hv_scope_includes_submitting_turn` (the foundation's rule that "the request's own turn is never a candidate, a dependency, or cited evidence", foundation section 3.1). A Code or Docs turn that needs HV before it can complete is completed first with `hostileReview` `Other` (for example "HV requested hvr-..."), which the foundation already allows and never counts as an AGREE (foundation C8); finalization then replaces that `Other` with the HV result. Rationale: no turn changes status after it is frozen, so there is no close-inside-finalization path. Rejected: admitting in-progress turns with a declared close intent (draft 213, section 3.B), which adds a mechanism and still freezes a turn the model is working in.
148: - R-06 Hostile reviews are written only by the pipeline. On agent surfaces a `hostileReview` write may carry only `status` `Other` (with its required `otherNotes`); a write naming `Pass`, `Fail`, or `Running`, or carrying `hvVerdict`, is refused with 403 `review_hostile_pipeline_only` (amendment A-06). Process ConvertHvReceiptToReview is retired. Rationale: a manual Pass or Fail would bypass reviewer exclusion, complete evidence, and atomic finalization, and no surface may bypass them (draft 213, H5, adopted). Rejected: keeping the manual route for emergencies; a reviewer can be enabled and checked instead (S-27).
149: - R-07 Assignment at admission, durable round-robin. The submit transaction picks the next eligible reviewer after the workspace's round-robin cursor and advances the cursor in the same SerializableWrite (policy RoundRobinAssignment), so assignment survives restarts and two concurrent submissions never pick from the same cursor value. When the assigned reviewer is no longer eligible at claim time (offline, disabled), the claim reassigns through the same policy and records the reassignment. Rejected: assignment at claim only, which hides the assignee from the submitter and lets claim order, not round-robin order, pick reviewers.
150: - R-08 One agent identity, server-attributed. `AgentIdentity` (namespace `QBrainAi.Client.Agents`, shared by the server, the REPL, and, through the golden contract, the PowerShell core) maps every known alias to one of the five reviewer ids: Claude (`claude`, `claudecode`, `claude-code`, `claudecowork`, `claude-cowork`, `cowork`), Codex (`codex`), Copilot (`copilot`), Grok (`grok`, `grokcode`, `grok-code`, `grokbot`, `grok-bot`), Cline (`cline`, `cline-v2`, `clinev2`), case-insensitively and ignoring separators. The submitter is the agent of the submitting turn, located by its full turn key (TurnLocator); a free-text name never overrides it. The author is the agent of the reviewed session (one request names turns of one MCP session, R-26), stored normalized as `AuthorReviewerId`. A reviewer whose id equals the submitter's or the author's is never eligible (S-17, S-28, P-01, P-07). Develop holds three alias maps with different canonical forms (`src/QBrainAi.Repl.Host/MarkerFileClientOptionsResolver.cs:64-81`, `src/QBrainAi.Repl.Core/TodoSelectionStore.cs:166-171`, the plugin's `Get-ReplCanonicalAgentName`); they are context under the DRY ruling and are not changed by this amendment. Exclusion is by agent family, not by model vendor (D-01, settled): S-17 names "the agent submitting the review", P-01 constrains the agent family and asks separately for the agent and the model, and the operator runs Cline on `gpt-6-astra` (provider `openai-codex`, VI-01 receipt) while keeping Cline and Codex as two reviewers (S-02); a model a reviewer shares with the submitter stays visible in the run's provenance, and the operator can disable that reviewer (UpdateHvReviewerCommand). Exclusion covers the author as well as the submitter (D-05, settled): a review by the agent that wrote the turns is a self-review, which S-28 rules out of HV and P-07 rules out of validation.
151: - R-09 Operator submissions. A caller with no session-log turn (Director, an operator at the REPL) submits with `submitter.kind` `Operator` and a name; no reviewer is excluded for the submitter, and the author of the reviewed session is still excluded (R-08). Agent surfaces (plugin verbs, MCP tools, the REPL workflow verb) always send the submitting turn's key, which the plugin binds automatically (foundation process BindVerbToTurn). Limit (section 8): every caller holds the same workspace key, so the server cannot prove that an `Operator` submission did not come from an agent.
152: - R-10 Readiness through NONCE (S-15, S-27). A reviewer is `Unverified`, `Online`, or `Offline`, and separately enabled or disabled. "NONCE the agent" is a probe run of the reviewer through its adapter with a fresh random nonce: it passes when the reviewer answers with the probe record that echoes the nonce and the adapter's runtime provenance shows the reviewer's resolved model and effort (P-04). Only a passing NONCE moves a reviewer to `Online`. An execution failure moves it to `Offline` until a later NONCE passes. The worker host NONCEs every enabled `Unverified` reviewer at startup and after a configuration change; an `Offline` reviewer is NONCEd only when a caller asks (S-15: "until resolved"). Rejected: a liveness ping or the server health nonce, which S-27 rules out.
153: - R-11 No execution time limit (P-02). A run has no timeout and no deadline. Liveness is the worker's lease, renewed by heartbeats; a stalled run stays visible (`lastOutputUtc`, the last progress record) and anyone can cancel it (S-18). The only expiry is the lease of a dead worker (R-13). This replaces the 30-minute `ExecutionTimeout` of the separate HostileReview options (`src/QBrainAi.Services/Options/HostileReviewWorkerOptions.cs:45-46`) for HV runs only. The process exit code is never the outcome of a run: the reviewer's records decide it (V-8 for a review, policy ReadinessProbeVerdict for a probe), because a CLI can end a refused or empty run with exit code 0 (VI-03: a headless Grok run whose write call was refused ended `cancelled` with exit 0, and two Copilot permission variants exited 0 with no output).
154: - R-12 True live output (S-22, P8). Each reviewer adapter delivers every output line as the process writes it, through a line callback, never after the process ends; the worker appends lines in batches (at most `OutputFlushInterval`, default 250 ms, or `OutputFlushBytes`, default 64 KiB, whichever comes first) through AppendHvRunOutputCommand, which stores each batch as one GZIP chunk and wakes the streams. The output stream replays stored chunks and then follows new ones (shared component OrderedEventReplay). Develop's one-shot strategy yields its output only after completion (`src/QBrainAi.Services/Services/OneShotCliAgentExecutionStrategy.cs:57-75`), so the adapters need a real line path (section 21, P8). Acceptance criterion FR-MCP-HVPIPE-008-AC003 makes the difference testable: a line is observable on the stream while the reviewer process is still running. The reviewer's records are read from each agent message's complete text, assembled from the CLI's native events (Grok's `streaming-json` sends message text one token per event, and Copilot sends deltas and then the whole message, as the probe runs of 2026-10-16 show), by one extraction function that the worker runs as lines arrive and finalization runs over the stored log (section 16.3), so a record split across events is read exactly once and both read the same records (FR-MCP-HVPIPE-010-AC006).
155: - R-13 Leases and fences (handoff requirement 10). A run is owned through a lease (owner, expiry) and a fence token that increases on every claim and takeover, the pattern develop already uses for handoff ingestion (owner and expiry with a `StateVersion` takeover, `src/QBrainAi.Services/Services/HandoffIngestionService.cs:724-735`, and a fenced terminal write that matches owner and version, `:782-807`). Every worker write carries the fence; a write with a stale fence changes nothing and returns `stale_fence`, and the worker that receives it stops its process. Expired leases are swept (ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand): the attempt becomes `Abandoned` and the request is queued again until `MaxAttemptsPerRequest` (default 3) is spent, then `Failed`, or `Canceled` when a cancel was requested; policy HvRetryDecision writes that outcome, with its turn release and its notification, for the sweep exactly as for FailHvRunCommand. Rejected: the unused lease options of the HostileReview subsystem (`HostileReviewWorkerOptions.cs:30-46`), which no code reads (section 21, P1).
156: - R-14 Evidence in the relational store, GZIP at rest (S-13, S-29, S-30). The accepted request is one GZIP blob written at admission; the response log is the run's ordered GZIP chunks; the result document is one GZIP blob written at finalization. No uncompressed copy of an evidence item is stored in the evidence tables, and each evidence item is stored there once (the structured rows of section 12, such as the request's `Context` and the findings, are records the units derive, not copies of the evidence blobs). The audit ledger keeps its own history of every evidence write, as it does for every audited entity: develop's ledger snapshots every property of an audited entity, binary columns included (`src/QBrainAi.Storage/McpDbContext.cs:1540-1589`), compressed with GZIP (`src/QBrainAi.Storage/Entities/DataAuditLogEntity.cs:119-147`), and a removal never changes it (R-20, I-13). Retrieval returns `application/gzip` (download name `<hvRequestId>-<kind>.jsonl.gz` or `.json.gz`) or, when asked, the decompressed bytes. The pattern is develop's audit ledger, which stores GZIP payloads in the database (`src/QBrainAi.Storage/Entities/DataAuditLogEntity.cs:66-147`). Rationale: S-23 ("Single trx at end") and S-29 (the database audit log) both hold only when the evidence is in the same transactional store as the result, and no crash window between a file system and the database remains. Rejected: `.jsonl.gz` files beside the database, which would need a two-store protocol, keep evidence outside the audit ledger, and split backups.
157: - R-15 Atomic finalization (S-23). FinalizeHvRequestCommand verifies the evidence and the reviewer output before it opens a transaction, then commits in one SerializableWrite: the result document, the per-turn assessments, the holistic evaluation, the failures, each turn's `hostileReview` through policy HvVerdictMapping (origin `HvFinalization`), each turn's `Final` HV state, the linked responses' model grades and trust decisions (when Mode is not `Off`), the request's `Completed` state, its notification, and the audit rows. The transaction re-checks everything the earlier reads relied on (the run's fence, the chunk manifest, the request and turn states). Crash windows are in section 9.
158: - R-16 Transactional notification outbox (S-19). Every state change that callers observe writes an `HvNotification` row in its own transaction, numbered by a per-workspace sequence that the same transaction advances, so the sequence has no gaps and no row is visible before its change commits. The notification stream replays rows after the caller's `Last-Event-ID` and then follows new ones (OrderedEventReplay). Delivery is at least once; consumers deduplicate by sequence. `IChangeEventBus` (develop's in-memory bus, `src/QBrainAi.Services/Notifications/IChangeEventBus.cs:4`) is used only to wake waiting streams and the worker, never as the record.
159: - R-17 Incidents through the triage endpoint (S-15, S-26). An execution failure writes an `HvIncident` row in the failure's transaction; FileHvIncidentCommand then submits it through `ITriageService` with its `dedupeKey` (`hv-reviewer-<reviewerId>-<failureCode>` for a failure attributable to the reviewer, `hv-server-<failureCode>` otherwise, section 12), which triage groups as `dedupe:<key>` (`src/QBrainAi.Services/Services/TriageService.cs:1475-1476`), and records the returned report and group ids. A filing that fails stays `Pending` and is retried by the worker host's sweep. Rejected: new incident tables with their own deduplication (S-26: "File through endpoint").
160: - R-18 Honest ETA (S-18, P-03). The ETA a caller sees is the reviewer's own latest progress record (`percentComplete`, `etaSeconds`), with `etaStatus` `Reported` and the record's time; with no progress record it is `etaStatus` `Unknown` and no number. The server never estimates.
161: - R-19 Audit participation and hard stop (S-29). Every HV entity carries `IsDeleted`, so `McpDbContext` writes its ledger rows for every HV mutation in the same `SaveChanges` (develop audits only entities with that property, `src/QBrainAi.Storage/McpDbContext.cs:1620-1627`). The ledger is append-only for HV: no HV unit or process updates or deletes a ledger row (I-13). Because develop skips the ledger when the audit table is unavailable (`McpDbContext.cs:1507-1538`), every HV unit first calls the shared component AuditLedgerGuard, which refuses with 503 `audit_unavailable` and writes nothing when the ledger cannot be written. Evidence reads (GetHvEvidenceQuery, GetHvResultQuery, and the output stream) write an explicit `read` ledger row before returning bytes, and a read whose row cannot be written is refused (the "protected-log access" of draft 213 participates in the audit log, S-29).
162: - R-20 Retention until removal (S-29). No unit deletes, expires, or compacts HV evidence except RemoveHvEvidenceCommand, an explicit call that removes the evidence bytes of one request, keeps its result rows, hashes, and sizes, records who removed it and why, and is audited. It clears the evidence tables only and never changes or deletes an audit ledger row: the ledger keeps the history of the evidence's writes and gains the record of the removal, because an audit log is never purged (I-13). There are no roles: any caller with the workspace key can call it, as S-29 requires.
163: - R-21 Self-review independence (S-28). No HV unit, policy, or process reads `agentReview`. The turn snapshot sent to a reviewer omits both review records (shared component TurnSnapshotBuilder), so a reviewer never sees a self-review grade. S-12 (a plugin list of missing agent reviews) is met by the foundation's Stop-gate remedy, which already lists each open turn's missing `agentReview` (foundation section 3.4, Stop gate, and `Get-CloseRemedy`, section 3.5.6), and is not an HV input. Reconciliation with the foundation's completion gate: HV admits only terminal turns (R-05), and the foundation's gate needs an `agentReview` status of `Pass`, `Fail`, or `Other` before a turn can close `completed` (foundation section 5.3, CompletionPolicy); that is a rule of closing a turn, not of HV, it is met by `Other` with a note as well as by a grade, and a turn closed `failed` or `canceled` needs no agent review at all; HV admission, execution, and verdict read none of it, and FR-MCP-HVPIPE-013 proves that every terminal turn is admitted and judged identically whatever its self-review.
164: - R-22 Verdict only (S-25). No HV unit writes TODO state. A result names the reviewed turns' `todoId` values for information only.
165: - R-23 Requirement references (S-14). The submitted context is stored as written (Markdown, YAML, or text, declared by `contextFormat`) and parsed for requirement references: FR, TR, and TEST ids of the form `<KIND>-<AREA>-<NNN>` with optional further dash-separated area segments, acceptance criteria written as `<FR id>-AC<NNN>` or `<FR id> ac-<n>`, and use cases by their store id or exact title. Each reference is resolved against the workspace's effective requirements and use cases and handed to the reviewer as a delineated list with its resolution status; an unresolved reference is listed as unresolved, never refused (shared component RequirementReferenceExtractor).
166: - R-24 The reviewer's own turn (P-06). The brief tells the reviewer to log its review as its own session-log turn, classified `Chore` so that its turn never needs an HV of its own (foundation completion policy: Chore needs no hostile review), and to store its entire result there. Finalization requires that turn to exist, to be persisted (not a failsafe or queued record), to have been created after the run started, and to contain the run's `hv_verdict` record byte for byte in its stored normal form (V-6). A reviewer whose host cannot log turns fails its NONCE with `reviewer_turn_logging_unsupported`. The reviewer's plugin runs as a host session of its own: a review or probe run never reads or changes the plugin state or the session-log session of a live session of the same agent in the workspace (FR-MCP-HVPIPE-008-AC008), which matters because a reviewer starts in the workspace (section 16.2) and Grok's headless hooks write their host state under the working directory's `.mcpServer/grok/` (VI-04).
167: - R-25 The HostileReview subsystem stays separate. FR-MCP-HOSTILEREVIEW-001 to -006 (its queue, artifact links, findings, and query surface) are not changed by this amendment, as the foundation already states (foundation section 5.4); the problems found in it (section 21, P1 to P3) are tracked in REMED-HVPIPELINE-001. It stays separate (D-02, settled): it reviews artifacts (TODO, FR/TR/TEST, plans, files, commits; FR-MCP-HOSTILEREVIEW-002) while this pipeline reviews session turns (S-03), the approved foundation keeps it separate, and consolidating it is scope the operator has not named. Its missing worker (P1) is built on this amendment's execution components (process HvWorkerHost and the reviewer adapters), so reviewer execution exists once (the DRY ruling).
168: - R-26 Scope limits. One request names turns of one MCP session. `MaxTurnsPerRequest` (default 200, the foundation's `HvRequest:MaxTurns` default) bounds every scope; a session scope above it is refused with 400 `hv_scope_too_large` naming the count, never truncated.
169: - R-27 One open review per turn. A turn is `Pending` in at most one open request (a unique filtered index on the turn key where the item is `Pending`); admission over a pending turn is refused with 409 `hv_turns_pending` naming the turns and their requests, and over a final turn with 409 `hv_turns_already_reviewed` (S-06, S-20).
170: - R-28 Cancellation by anyone (S-18). `Queued` becomes `Canceled` at once; `Running` becomes `CancelRequested`, and the worker stops the process at its next heartbeat and closes the run `Canceled`; `Finalizing`, `Completed`, `Failed`, and `Canceled` refuse with 409 `hv_request_not_cancelable`. A cancel and a finalization of the same request are serialized on the request row, so exactly one of them commits.
171: - R-29 Worker units are internal. ClaimHvRunCommand, RecordHvRunHeartbeatCommand, AppendHvRunOutputCommand, CloseHvRunOutputCommand, FailHvRunCommand, ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand, FinalizeHvRequestCommand, and FileHvIncidentCommand have no REST route, MCP tool, or client method; only the worker host dispatches them, in-process, through `IDispatcher`. The public mutations are submit, cancel, reviewer update, NONCE, and evidence removal.
172: - R-30 Plugins consume notifications through the REPL. Plugins never call REST (foundation section 3); the REPL gains a streaming verb that follows the notification stream, and the PowerShell core runs it in the background per host session (process WatchHvNotifications), keeping the last sequence in the host session's state and handing completions of requests that host session submitted to the next prompt as context.
173: - R-31 The 98/98 bar for the overall verdict (P-05). The overall verdict is `AGREE` only when the holistic correctness and completeness both meet `max(configured hostile threshold, 0.98)` (ScoreVerdict, foundation section 3.5.4) and no failure is FAIL or UNKNOWN; per-turn hostile reviews keep the foundation's configured hostile thresholds through HvVerdictMapping.

192: ## 7. Lifecycles
193: 
194: ### 7.1 HV request
195: 
196: ```mermaid
197: stateDiagram-v2
198:     [*] --> Queued: SubmitHvRequestCommand, turns frozen Pending
199:     Queued --> Running: ClaimHvRunCommand, run attempt claimed
200:     Queued --> Canceled: CancelHvRequestCommand
201:     Running --> Queued: attempt Failed or Abandoned, attempts left
202:     Running --> CancelRequested: CancelHvRequestCommand
203:     CancelRequested --> Canceled: worker stops the process, or the lease expires
204:     Running --> Finalizing: CloseHvRunOutputCommand, output closed
205:     Finalizing --> Completed: FinalizeHvRequestCommand commits, turns Final
206:     Finalizing --> Queued: verification failed, attempts left
207:     Running --> Failed: attempts spent
208:     Finalizing --> Failed: verification failed, attempts spent
209:     Canceled --> [*]: turns released to None
210:     Failed --> [*]: turns released to None
211:     Completed --> [*]
212: ```
213: 
214: - `Queued` and `Running` hold the turns `Pending`. `Completed`, `Failed`, and `Canceled` are terminal and never change again (S-06, S-20). A request whose attempt fails returns to `Queued` with its assignment re-evaluated (R-07); with no eligible reviewer it stays `Queued`, its ETA `Unknown`, until a reviewer passes a NONCE or the request is canceled, so no work is lost to an outage.
215: - `CancelRequested` is not terminal: the request is canceled when the worker has stopped the process or when the lease of a dead worker expires.
216: 
217: ### 7.2 Run attempt
218: 
219: ```mermaid
220: stateDiagram-v2
221:     [*] --> Claimed: ClaimHvRunCommand, lease and fence
222:     Claimed --> Running: worker started the reviewer process
223:     Running --> Running: heartbeat renews the lease, output appended
224:     Running --> OutputClosed: CloseHvRunOutputCommand
225:     Running --> Failed: FailHvRunCommand, execution failure
226:     Running --> Canceled: cancel observed at a heartbeat
227:     Claimed --> Abandoned: lease expired, ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand
228:     Running --> Abandoned: lease expired, ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand
229:     OutputClosed --> Succeeded: FinalizeHvRequestCommand committed, or probe passed
230:     OutputClosed --> Failed: verification failed, or probe failed

1: # Agent Instructions
2: 
3: ## Session Start
4: 
5: 1. Read `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml` in the repo root for the current API key and endpoints.
6: 2. For specific operational steps (session bootstrap, session log turn workflow, and helper command sequence), follow `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml`.
7: 
8: On every subsequent user message:
9: 
10: 1. Follow `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml` for specific operational instructions.
11: 2. Complete the user's request.
12: 
13: ## Rules
14: 
15: 1. `templates/prompt-templates.yaml` (`default-marker-prompt`) is the source of truth for specific agent instructions. `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml` is the rendered runtime instruction set.
16: 2. Keep this file focused on durable workspace policy and conventions; avoid duplicating marker-file operational procedures.
17: 3. Use helper modules for session log and TODO operations. Do not make raw API calls.
18: 4. Persist session log updates immediately after each meaningful change (turn creation, action append, decision, requirement, blocker, file/context update). Do not defer saves.
19: 5. Capture rich turn detail: interpretation, response, status, actions (type/status/filePath), contextList, filesModified, designDecisions, requirementsDiscovered, blockers, and relevant processing dialog.
20: 6. Follow workspace conventions in `.github/copilot-instructions.md` for build, test, and architecture guidance.
21: 7. Use **only `pwsh.exe`** for shell commands and script execution; do not use `powershell.exe`.
22: 8. When you need API schemas, module examples, or compliance rules, load them from `docs/context/` or use `context_search`.
23: 9. Do not fabricate information. If you made a mistake, acknowledge it. Distinguish facts from speculation.
24: 10. Prioritize correctness over speed. Do not ship code you have not verified compiles and is logically sound.
25: 11. When writing session logs or other audit records, agents must identify themselves accurately using their real agent identity in Pascal-Case. Do not use placeholder, legacy, or misleading sourceType values.
26: 12. Never edit YAML by appending, replacing, or removing text lines. Deserialize the complete document into an object, mutate the object, serialize it, and save it. Use `plugins/core/lib-ps/yaml-object-mutation.ps1` for PowerShell work.
27: 
28: ## Byrd Test Gate
29: 
30: The canonical process is `docs/Development-Process-draft-v4.md`. To leave a Byrd implementation slice, the entire unit test suite for the current iteration and previous iterations must be completely passing. In this workspace, skipped tests are not passing tests: a validation gate requires zero failures and zero skips in the executed scope. Tests should directly track progress; deferred work belongs in MCP TODO/requirements state until that slice starts, not in skipped test placeholders.
31: 
32: ## Where Things Live
33: 
34: - `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml` — connection details, API key, workspace config (regenerated on server start)
35: - `.github/copilot-instructions.md` — build/test commands, architecture overview, coding conventions
36: - `docs/context/` — on-demand reference docs (schemas, module docs, compliance rules, action types)
37: - `docs/Project/` — requirements docs, TODO.yaml, mapping matrices
38: - `templates/` — prompt templates (loaded on demand)
39: - `tools/powershell/McpContext.psm1` — PowerShell module for context ingestion/query workflows
40: - `tools/powershell/McpContext.USER.md` — user-level guide for the McpContext module
41: - `tools/powershell/McpContext.AGENT.md` — agent workflow instructions for the McpContext module
42: - `plugins/core/lib-ps/yaml-object-mutation.ps1` — object-first YAML mutation helper for agents and plugin maintenance
43: 
44: ## MCP Interaction via REPL Tools
45: 
46: Agents running inside `McpAgent` must use the 27 built-in tools instead of raw HTTP calls. See `docs/REPL-MIGRATION-GUIDE.md` for the full tool inventory and migration patterns.
47: 
48: Key rules:
49: - Use `mcp_session_*` tools for session log lifecycle (bootstrap, turns, history).
50: - Use `mcp_todo_*` tools for TODO CRUD (query, get, create, update, delete, plan, status, implementation).
51: - Use `mcp_requirements_*` tools for FR/TR/TEST queries.
52: - Use `mcp_client_invoke` for any sub-client method not covered by a dedicated tool (context search, GitHub, workspace, etc.).
53: - Do not make raw HTTP calls to `/qbrainai/*` endpoints when a tool is available.
54: 
55: ## Context Loading by Task Type
56: 
57: - Agent Help: see marker `## Agent Help (QBrain.AI issues)` in `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml`; API `/qbrainai/agent-help`
58: - Session logging → `docs/context/session-log-schema.md` + `docs/context/module-bootstrap.md`

62: - Logging actions → `docs/context/action-types.md`
63: - New to workspace → this file + `docs/context/api-capabilities.md`
64: - Migrating from raw API → `docs/REPL-MIGRATION-GUIDE.md`

66: ## Agent Conduct
67: 
68: You represent the workspace owner. Your work directly reflects the owner's professional reputation.
69: 
70: ### Honesty
71: 
72: - Do not fabricate information, capabilities, or results.
73: - Distinguish between facts, informed opinions, and speculation.
74: - Acknowledge mistakes immediately and correct them.
75: 
76: ### Correctness
77: 
78: - Prioritize correctness over speed.
79: - When uncertain, state your uncertainty and suggest verification steps.
80: - Prefer proven patterns over clever approaches unless directed otherwise.
81: - All code must have XMLDocs. All public APIs must be documented.
82: - Follow DRY, SOLID, and existing project conventions.
83: 
84: ### Decision Documentation
85: 
86: - Log every decision to the session log, including trivial ones.
87: - For each decision, document: what was decided, why, what alternatives were considered, what was rejected.
88: - Log design decisions as dialog entries with category "decision" and as session log actions with type "design_decision".
89: 
90: ### Professional Representation
91: 
92: - Every interaction is audited via the session log.
93: - Every commit must be correct, clean, well-described, and complete.
94: - Log all commits as actions with type "commit" (SHA, branch, message, files).
95: - Log all PR/issue comments as actions with type "pr_comment" or "issue_comment".
96: - Always sign PR comments using the same signature convention as commits, identifying the actual authoring agent.
97: 
98: ### Source Attribution
99: 
100: - Document all web sources in the session log as actions with type "web_reference" (URL, title, usage).
101: - Add source URLs to the turn's contextList array.
102: - Attribute external code in both the session log and code comments.
103: 
104: ## Requirements Tracking
105: 
106: When you discover or agree on new requirements during a session:
107: 
108: 1. Update the files in `docs/Project/`:
109:    - `Functional-Requirements.md` — append FR-MCP-* entries
110:    - `Technical-Requirements.md` — append TR-MCP-* entries
111:    - `TR-per-FR-Mapping.md` — append mapping rows
112:    - `Requirements-Matrix.md` — append status rows
113:    - `Testing-Requirements.md` — append TEST-MCP-* entries
114: 2. Include the requirement ID in your session log turn's tags.
115: 3. Capture requirements as they emerge. Do not defer to later.
116: 
117: ## Design Decision Logging
118: 
119: When a design decision is made:
120: 
121: 1. Log it as a session log dialog item with category "decision".
122: 2. Include: the decision, alternatives considered, rationale, and affected requirements.
123: 3. Add a session log action with type "design_decision".
124: 4. If the decision affects existing code or requirements, note what needs updating.
125: 
126: ## Session Continuity
127: 
128: At the start of every session:
129: 
130: 1. Follow the session-start checklist in `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml`.
131: 2. Read `docs/Project/Requirements-Matrix.md` to understand project state.
132: 3. If resuming interrupted work, review the last session's pending decisions.
133: 
134: At regular intervals during long sessions (~10 interactions):
135: 
136: 1. Follow marker-file update cadence and session logging requirements from `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml`.
137: 2. Ensure all design decisions are captured.
138: 3. Verify requirements docs are up to date.
139: 
140: ## Glossary
141: 
142: - **MCP** — Model Context Protocol, an open standard for tool-calling between AI agents and context servers.
143: - **Workspace** — a project directory registered with the MCP server. All workspaces share a single port; use the `X-Workspace-Path` header to target a specific one.
144: - **Marker File** — the `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml` file at each workspace root. Contains connection details, auth token, and agent prompt.
145: - **API Key** — a per-workspace cryptographic token that rotates on each server restart. Required for all `/qbrainai/*` REST endpoints.
146: - **Streamable HTTP** — the MCP wire protocol transport at `/mcp-transport`. Carries JSON-RPC tool calls over HTTP POST with streaming responses.
147: - **Session Log** — an audit record of every agent interaction, stored per-session with full request/response history.
148: - **Context Pack** — an ordered set of document chunks retrieved by semantic + full-text hybrid search, scoped to the workspace.
149: - **Tool Bucket** — a GitHub repository containing tool manifest files, similar to a Scoop package bucket.
150: 
151: ## Response Formatting
152: 
153: - Do not use table-style output in responses.
154: - Use concise bullets or short paragraphs instead.

46: ## Architecture
47: 
48: **QBrainAi** is an ASP.NET Core 9 server (.NET 9.0) providing workspace-scoped context retrieval, TODO management, session logging, repository operations, GraphRAG, and GitHub automation for AI agents.
49: 
50: ### Transports
51: 
52: - **HTTP REST** — Controllers at `/qbrainai/*` in `src/QBrainAi.Support.Mcp/Controllers/`
53: - **MCP Streamable HTTP** — JSON-RPC wire protocol at `/mcp-transport`
54: - **MCP STDIO** — `--transport stdio` flag; tools in `McpStdio/FwhMcpTools.cs`
55: 
56: ### Workspace Model
57: 
58: A single host process manages multiple workspaces. Each workspace gets its own in-process Kestrel `WebApplication` via `WorkspaceAppFactory` (not child processes). The primary workspace is served directly by the host. Workspace targeting uses the `X-Workspace-Path` header. Config lives in `appsettings.yaml` under `Mcp:Workspaces`. Per-instance overrides: `Mcp:Instances:{name}:*` resolved by `McpInstanceResolver`.
59: 
60: ### Search Pipeline
61: 
62: Hybrid search combining SQLite FTS5 full-text with HNSW vector similarity (384-dim all-MiniLM-L6-v2 ONNX embeddings). `HybridSearchService` fuses results with BM25 scoring.
63: 
64: ### Storage
65: 
66: EF Core with SQLite (`McpDbContext`), with migration projects for SQLite, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server. TODO items live in the configured database as the sole source of truth; `docs/Project/TODO.yaml` is a read-only projection. `Mcp:TodoStorage:Provider` accepts `database` (`sqlite` is a deprecated alias; the removed `yaml` value fails fast per TR-MCP-CFG-007).
67:

69: 
70: - `QBrainAi.Support.Mcp` — main server application
71: - `QBrainAi.Services` — ingestion, context search, models
72: - `QBrainAi.Storage` — EF Core with SQLite FTS5 + HNSW vector search
73: - `QBrainAi.Cqrs` — CQRS command/query handlers
74: - `QBrainAi.McpAgent` — agent hosting & tool execution framework
75: - `QBrainAi.Client` — typed REST client (published as NuGet `QBrainAI.Client`)
76: - `QBrainAi.GraphRag` — GraphRAG indexing & query (workspace-scoped, disabled by default)

119: ## MCP Session Logging — Mandatory Precondition
120: 
121: **Speed is never more important than following workspace procedures.**
122: 
123: ### Session Start (Run Once Per Session)
124: 
125: 1. **Read `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml`** in the repo root for the current API key, endpoints, and base URL
126: 2. **Bootstrap the required plugin interface** before any state-changing MCP call. For Claude Code, use the `mcpserver-claude-code-plugin` wrapper and its `workflow.*` / `client.*` methods. "Not in the visible tool list" does not mean unavailable; use the documented wrapper invocation form.
127: 3. **Verify marker signature and health** through the required plugin status/bootstrap path. Use direct REST only for read-only diagnosis after the documented plugin path fails.
128: 4. **Review recent session history and current TODOs** through the required plugin only after verification succeeds
129: 5. **POST an initial session log turn** through the required plugin
130: 6. **THEN** begin working on the user's request
131: 
132: If signature verification, `/health`, or nonce verification fails: log `MCP_UNTRUSTED`, continue without the MCP server, and do not probe additional MCP endpoints.
133: 
134: ### Per User Message
135: 
136: 1. POST a new session log turn BEFORE starting work
137: 2. Complete the user's request
138: 3. Update the turn with results, actions taken, and files modified when done
139: 
140: ### Re-run Full Session Start Only If
141: 
142: - The user explicitly says "Start Session"
143: - Signature verification fails
144: - `/health` fails or nonce verification fails
145: - Any `/qbrainai/*` call returns 401
146: - The marker endpoint/key changes after a server restart
147: 
148: ### Authentication
149: 
150: All `/qbrainai/*` endpoints require a per-workspace auth token (from `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml`). These details are for plugin internals, typed client integration, and read-only diagnosis after plugin failure; they are not permission to bypass the required plugin route for session log, TODO, requirements, import/export, or traceability operations:
151: - Header: `X-Api-Key: <token>`
152: - Or query param: `?api_key=<token>`
153: - If you receive a 401, re-read the marker file — the token rotates on each server restart
154: 
155: ### Session Log Rules
156: 
157: - Use rich turn detail: interpretation, response, status, actions (type/status/filePath), contextList, filesModified, designDecisions, requirementsDiscovered, blockers, and key processingDialog
158: - Persist session log updates immediately after each meaningful change — do not defer saves
159: - Before any compaction step, persist the current session log state; after compaction, update again to record the outcome
160: - Agents must identify themselves accurately using their real agent identity in Pascal-Case (e.g., `ClaudeCode`). Do not use placeholder or misleading sourceType values
161: 
162: ### Naming Conventions
163: 
164: - **TODO IDs**: uppercase canonical form `<SDLC-PHASE>-<AREA>-###` (e.g., `PLAN-NAMINGCONVENTIONS-001`) or `ISSUE-{number}`. Never write to `TODO.yaml` directly
165: - **Session IDs**: `<Agent>-<yyyyMMddTHHmmssZ>-<suffix>` with Pascal-Case agent prefix
166: - **Request IDs**: `req-<yyyyMMddTHHmmssZ>-<slugOrOrdinal>`, unique within a session

46: ## Architecture
47: 
48: **QBrainAi** is an ASP.NET Core 9 server (.NET 9.0) providing workspace-scoped context retrieval, TODO management, session logging, repository operations, GraphRAG, and GitHub automation for AI agents.
49: 
50: ### Transports
51: 
52: - **HTTP REST** — Controllers at `/qbrainai/*` in `src/QBrainAi.Support.Mcp/Controllers/`
53: - **MCP Streamable HTTP** — JSON-RPC wire protocol at `/mcp-transport`
54: - **MCP STDIO** — `--transport stdio` flag; tools in `McpStdio/FwhMcpTools.cs`
55: 
56: ### Workspace Model
57: 
58: A single host process manages multiple workspaces. Each workspace gets its own in-process Kestrel `WebApplication` via `WorkspaceAppFactory` (not child processes). The primary workspace is served directly by the host. Workspace targeting uses the `X-Workspace-Path` header. Config lives in `appsettings.yaml` under `Mcp:Workspaces`. Per-instance overrides: `Mcp:Instances:{name}:*` resolved by `McpInstanceResolver`.
59: 
60: ### Search Pipeline
61: 
62: Hybrid search combining SQLite FTS5 full-text with HNSW vector similarity (384-dim all-MiniLM-L6-v2 ONNX embeddings). `HybridSearchService` fuses results with BM25 scoring.
63: 
64: ### Storage
65: 
66: EF Core with SQLite (`McpDbContext`), with migration projects for SQLite, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server. TODO items live in the configured database as the sole source of truth; `docs/Project/TODO.yaml` is a read-only projection. `Mcp:TodoStorage:Provider` accepts `database` (`sqlite` is a deprecated alias; the removed `yaml` value fails fast per TR-MCP-CFG-007).
67: 
68: ### Key Projects
69: 
70: - `QBrainAi.Support.Mcp` — main server application
71: - `QBrainAi.Services` — ingestion, context search, models
72: - `QBrainAi.Storage` — EF Core with SQLite FTS5 + HNSW vector search
73: - `QBrainAi.Cqrs` — CQRS command/query handlers
74: - `QBrainAi.McpAgent` — agent hosting & tool execution framework
75: - `QBrainAi.Client` — typed REST client (published as NuGet `QBrainAI.Client`)
76: - `QBrainAi.GraphRag` — GraphRAG indexing & query (workspace-scoped, disabled by default)
77: - `QBrainAi.Repl.Core` / `QBrainAi.Repl.Host` — REPL command interpreter and dotnet tool
78:

81: - Unit tests: `QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.Tests`, `QBrainAi.Client.Tests`, `QBrainAi.Cqrs.Tests`, `QBrainAi.Launcher.Tests`, `QBrainAi.McpAgent.Tests`, `QBrainAi.Repl.Core.Tests`

119: ## MCP Session Logging — Mandatory Precondition
120: 
121: **Speed is never more important than following workspace procedures.**
122: 
123: ### Session Start (Run Once Per Session)
124: 
125: 1. **Read `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml`** in the repo root for the current API key, endpoints, and base URL
126: 2. **Bootstrap the required plugin interface** before any state-changing MCP call. For Claude Code, use the `mcpserver-claude-code-plugin` wrapper and its `workflow.*` / `client.*` methods. "Not in the visible tool list" does not mean unavailable; use the documented wrapper invocation form.
127: 3. **Verify marker signature and health** through the required plugin status/bootstrap path. Use direct REST only for read-only diagnosis after the documented plugin path fails.
128: 4. **Review recent session history and current TODOs** through the required plugin only after verification succeeds
129: 5. **POST an initial session log turn** through the required plugin
130: 6. **THEN** begin working on the user's request
131: 
132: If signature verification, `/health`, or nonce verification fails: log `MCP_UNTRUSTED`, continue without the MCP server, and do not probe additional MCP endpoints.
133: 
134: ### Per User Message
135: 
136: 1. POST a new session log turn BEFORE starting work
137: 2. Complete the user's request
138: 3. Update the turn with results, actions taken, and files modified when done
139: 
140: ### Re-run Full Session Start Only If
141: 
142: - The user explicitly says "Start Session"
143: - Signature verification fails
144: - `/health` fails or nonce verification fails
145: - Any `/qbrainai/*` call returns 401
146: - The marker endpoint/key changes after a server restart
147: 
148: ### Authentication
149: 
150: All `/qbrainai/*` endpoints require a per-workspace auth token (from `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml`). These details are for plugin internals, typed client integration, and read-only diagnosis after plugin failure; they are not permission to bypass the required plugin route for session log, TODO, requirements, import/export, or traceability operations:
151: - Header: `X-Api-Key: <token>`
152: - Or query param: `?api_key=<token>`
153: - If you receive a 401, re-read the marker file — the token rotates on each server restart
154: 
155: ### Session Log Rules
156: 
157: - Use rich turn detail: interpretation, response, status, actions (type/status/filePath), contextList, filesModified, designDecisions, requirementsDiscovered, blockers, and key processingDialog
158: - Persist session log updates immediately after each meaningful change — do not defer saves
159: - Before any compaction step, persist the current session log state; after compaction, update again to record the outcome
160: - Agents must identify themselves accurately using their real agent identity in Pascal-Case (e.g., `ClaudeCode`). Do not use placeholder or misleading sourceType values
161: 
162: ### Naming Conventions
163: 
164: - **TODO IDs**: uppercase canonical form `<SDLC-PHASE>-<AREA>-###` (e.g., `PLAN-NAMINGCONVENTIONS-001`) or `ISSUE-{number}`. Never write to `TODO.yaml` directly
165: - **Session IDs**: `<Agent>-<yyyyMMddTHHmmssZ>-<suffix>` with Pascal-Case agent prefix
166: - **Request IDs**: `req-<yyyyMMddTHHmmssZ>-<slugOrOrdinal>`, unique within a session
167: 
168: ## Agent Conduct
169: 
170: - Do not fabricate information. Acknowledge mistakes. Distinguish facts from speculation
171: - Prioritize correctness over speed. Do not ship code you have not verified compiles
172: - Log every decision to the session log, including: what was decided, why, alternatives considered, what was rejected
173: - Document all web sources as actions with type `web_reference`
174: - Do not use table-style output in responses — use concise bullets or short paragraphs
175: 
176: ## Requirements Tracking
177: 
178: When you discover or agree on new requirements during a session, update the files in `docs/Project/`:
179: - `Functional-Requirements.md` — append FR-MCP-* entries
180: - `Technical-Requirements.md` — append TR-MCP-* entries
181: - `TR-per-FR-Mapping.md` — append mapping rows
182: - `Requirements-Matrix.md` — append status rows
183: - `Testing-Requirements.md` — append TEST-MCP-* entries
184: 
185: Include the requirement ID in your session log turn's tags. Capture requirements as they emerge — do not defer.

210: ## QBrain.AI Claude Plugin and Hook Contract
211: 
212: Claude must treat QBrain.AI plugin and hook setup as a live runtime contract, not background documentation. On every new Claude session in this workspace, and whenever QBrain.AI behavior looks stale, incomplete, or inconsistent, perform this validation before relying on QBrain.AI workflows.
213: 
214: ### Required Startup Validation
215: 
216: 1. Read `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml` from the active workspace root and use it as the current source of truth for QBrain.AI endpoint, API key, workspace path, plugin instructions, and failure-reporting rules.
217: 2. Identify the active QBrain.AI Claude plugin cache path and version from the marker file, plugin manifest, or active wrapper path. Do not assume a previously cached path is current.
218: 3. Inspect `%USERPROFILE%\.claude\plugins\cache` for stale QBrain.AI plugin entries. Delete stale `mcpserver`, `mcpserver-*`, or `mcpserver-cowork` cache entries that are not the active plugin cache path/version for this session.
219: 4. Do not delete the active plugin cache path for the current session. If unsure which path is active, stop deleting and report the ambiguity.
220: 5. Reload or rebootstrap the active QBrain.AI Claude plugin after stale cache cleanup.
221: 6. Inspect Claude active settings, including user-level and workspace/session-level settings, and verify QBrain.AI hooks are actually installed in the active settings layer. Do not accept hook files existing in the plugin package as proof that hooks are active.
222: 7. If hooks are missing or stale, install or refresh them through the supported QBrain.AI Claude plugin hook validation skill or wrapper path.
223: 8. Verify the plugin wrapper/status command works and record the exact command or tool path used.
224: 9. Verify subprocesses launched by the plugin use the workspace root as process current working directory, not the inherited user profile directory.
225: 
226: ### Required Usage Rules
227: 
228: 1. Use supported QBrain.AI plugin wrappers, hooks, skills, or MCP tools for session logging, TODOs, requirements, triage, and status checks. Do not use raw REST when a supported wrapper, hook, skill, or MCP tool exists.
229: 2. Session logging must use the supported session wrapper or MCP tools and must create, update, and complete turns through the plugin flow.
230: 3. TODO operations must use the supported TODO wrapper, workflow, or MCP tools. Do not edit TODO storage directly.
231: 4. Requirements operations must use the supported requirements wrapper, workflow, or MCP tools. Do not edit requirements storage directly.
232: 5. Triage operations must use the supported triage wrapper, workflow, or MCP tools.
233: 6. QBrain.AI failures and plugin failures discovered while doing unrelated work must always be written as a normal failsafe YAML report through the plugin failsafe flow, then submitted through triage.
234: 7. If triage submission succeeds, Claude must continue the user active task without waiting for triage research or TODO creation. If triage submission fails, stop work and notify the user. Do not invent a raw REST fallback or alternate reporting channel.
235: 8. Normal plugin execution must use PowerShell only. Bash is allowed only for installing PowerShell. Node must not be used for JSON or YAML construction.
236: 9. JSON and YAML payloads must be built from native objects and serialized. Do not handwrite YAML or JSON as fragile string literals.
237: 10. If any validation check fails, report the exact failed check, the path or command involved, and the blocked capability. Do not claim QBrain.AI compliance until the check is fixed or explicitly marked unavailable.

Where a proposal conflicts with an operator statement, the operator statement governs: draft 161 allowed a later HV of an already reviewed turn ("new grade rows supersede"), which S-06, S-07, and S-20 forbid.

131: Ownership: the HostileValidation bounded context owns every unit, policy, entity, and process of this amendment. It calls the foundation's SessionTurnLogging (TurnLocator, TurnWritePipeline), TurnReviews (ScoreLexeme, ScoreVerdict, policy HvVerdictMapping), ResponsesAndTrust (RecordModelGradeCommand, DecideAgentResponseTrustCommand), and SharedComponents (SerializableWrite, IdempotentCreate, ReadableKeyAllocator, PagedQuery, ClassifiedErrorException, ContentHasher, SecretRedactor) through their Phase 2 seams, and the existing `ITriageService` (POST `/qbrainai/triage/reports`, `src/QBrainAi.Support.Mcp/Controllers/TriageController.cs:13-14,33`). Namespaces follow the foundation rule (foundation section 3.5): commands in `src/QBrainAi.Services/HostileValidation/Commands/` (namespace `QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.HostileValidation.Commands`), queries in `.../Queries/`, policies in `.../Policies/`, the worker in `.../Execution/`, adapters in `.../Reviewers/`, entities in `src/QBrainAi.Storage/Entities/HostileValidation/` (namespace `QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.Storage.Entities.HostileValidation`), DTOs in `src/QBrainAi.Client/Models/HostileValidation/` (namespace `QBrainAi.Client.Models.HostileValidation`), one type per file.

133: Trust boundaries:
134: 
135: - Callers authenticate with the workspace API key, as every route does; there are no access roles (S-29). Agent identity is therefore not authenticated by the server: the submitter's identity is the agent of the submitting turn the server finds (R-08), and the limit of that model is stated in section 8.
136: - The reviewer CLI is untrusted input to the server. Its output is evidence to verify, never an instruction; the server parses only the records the reviewer contract defines (section 13.3) and verifies them before anything is finalized (policy HvFinalVerification, section 15).
137: - Turn text sent to a reviewer passes through `SecretRedactor` (foundation section 3.5.2) before it leaves the server; the stored request evidence is the redacted brief exactly as sent.
